Is ARM better than x86 and x64? How reliable are benchmarks?
Why do benchmarks show processors in smartphones being as fast if not faster than the ones in laptops?

From what I understand they differ in quality based on how much temporary memory they have. A desktop capable of gaming or other more complex programs needs more ram than a phone would require. The processors are optimized for each machine in a different way. I may be wrong but that what I have come to understand.

Think of clockspeed (I.e. the mhz/ghz listed for a CPU) like the Revolutions Per Minute on an engine. Different types of engine might be capable of turning the same number of RPM, but they all do different amounts of work and are better suited to different tasks. My truck's engine will work a lot harder at 3,000 RPM than my Lawnmower will.

clockspeed is perhaps the worst means of comparing two different processors, much less different architectures.

Frankly, ARM is crap. ARM CPUs are small engines, like on a lawn tractor or motorcycle. Their main virtue is that they're power efficient. Which is great when you need to carry it around in your pocket, and power it off a tiny battery. This is why they're big in phones and tablets. They're not necessarily good at heavy workloads though.

x86/x64 are much more potent workhorses, but they are crap at power efficiency. But, you really can't lump all of them together like that, there is a gigantic range of different options all under the umbrella of "x86/x64". You can't expect to compare a chip at a particular speed with another one, and get an accurate result, especially since we've been kinda limited in how high we can push chips for awhile. For the last decade and a half, most CPUs have been between 2.5ghz and 4ghz. But the Celeron 2.8ghz laptop CPU I had in 2006 is significantly weaker than the 6 core Phenom II I owned at roughly the same speed. Think of this whole family as encompassing everything from passenger cars to pickup trucks, to boats and airplanes.

Additionally, we've surpassed the average computer user's needs for computing. You no longer need the latest and greatest cutting edge technology to basic tasks. Hell, you don't even NEED it to game.

Benchmarks, meanwhile, have their own problems. Most of them reflect favorably on multi-core performance, but this doesn't always translate to real-world usage.

For example, look at the last 3 generations of AMD chips. The Phenom II chips were 1 thread per core (Basically, each core could only work on one task at a time) and they were succeeded by the FX series of chips. These had a different type of core, that was basically two copies of the front half of the core, that shared a common back-end. They didn't do a great job of implementing this though, and unless you are doing certain specific tasks, their performance is kind of garbage. Then there's their new "Ryzen" chips, which have a MUCH better implementation of the multi-threaded cores.

For most tasks, the Phenom II, based on ~2009 technology would outperform the FX chip, sometimes to a ridiculous degree, but the new Ryzen chips put both of them to shame, and this is hard to represent in benchmarks, most of which show the FX chip as "better" than the Phenom II, because most benchmarks reward having lots of cores.

So, benchmarks are useful, but not absolute. It pays to know what the nature of the task you're trying to run is. Most older games made poor use of extra cores/threads, but newer games are getting better and better at it.
